narration.text: Welcome to the section on intersections and turning. This first lesson covers how to approach any intersection. The guide defines what an intersection is, notes that every intersection is legally a crosswalk, and lists the checks to make before you enter. It also covers what to do when your view is blocked, the rule against blocking an intersection, and places where you should scan with extra care. To remember: what counts as an intersection; checks before entering; not blocking and scanning. A helpful hook for this lesson: stop at the line, then creep.

lines.text: Anywhere two or more roads meet.

narration.text: An intersection is any spot where two or more roads meet. That includes cross streets, roundabouts, calming circles, side streets, driveways and shopping center or parking lot entrances. Every intersection is legally a crosswalk, whether or not a crosswalk is painted. So the rules for intersections and crosswalks apply in many more places than just corners with traffic lights. To remember: anywhere two or more roads meet; includes driveways and lot entrances; every intersection is a crosswalk. A helpful hook for this lesson: stop at the line, then creep.

lines.text: Yield to pedestrians and traffic in it.
Look each way more than once.

narration.text: Before entering an intersection, yield to pedestrians and to traffic already in it. Look each way more than once. Check your mirrors and over your shoulder for cyclists, motorcyclists or walkers entering your path. Do not start across or into a turn unless there is room to finish without blocking the intersection. These checks come before every entry, whether or not there is a signal. To remember: yield to pedestrians and traffic in it; look each way more than once; mirrors and shoulder for cyclists, walkers. A helpful hook for this lesson: stop at the line, then creep.

lines.text: Stop at the stop line first.

narration.text: If your view of the cross street is blocked after stopping at the stop line, creep forward slowly until you can see. This also lets crossing drivers spot your front end first. Stopping at the stop line comes first, and creeping slowly forward is a second step used only when the view of the cross street is still blocked. So the stop line is never skipped; the creep comes after it. To remember: stop at the stop line first; then creep forward slowly; crossing drivers see your front end. A helpful hook for this lesson: stop at the line, then creep.

lines.text: Trap: creep past the line instead.

narration.text: Here is the trap. When a driver cannot see past parked cars or bushes, it is tempting to roll past the stop line without stopping. The guide sets the order: stopping at the stop line comes first, and creeping slowly forward is a second step used only when the view of the cross street is still blocked. So a question that skips the stop and goes straight to creeping is describing the wrong order. To remember: stop at the line first; creep only if still blocked. A helpful hook for this lesson: stop at the line, then creep.

Here is a quick check: you stopped at the stop line and you still cannot see the cross street because of parked vehicles. What do you do next? Decide before the answer. The answer is to creep forward slowly until you can see. Stopping at the stop line comes first, and creeping forward is the next step when the view is still blocked, which also lets crossing drivers spot your front end first. A helpful hook for this lesson: stop at the line, then creep. In short: stopping at the stop line comes first, and creeping slowly forward is the next step when the view is still blocked.

lines.text: Stop, creep if blocked; never block.

narration.text: To wrap up, an intersection is any spot where roads meet, including driveways and parking lot entrances, and every intersection is legally a crosswalk. Before entering, yield to pedestrians and traffic already in it, look each way more than once, and check mirrors and shoulders. Stop at the line and creep forward only if the view is still blocked. Never start across without room to finish, and scan with extra care near shopping centers, construction, parks, playgrounds and schoolyards. To remember: roads meet, crosswalk exists; yield, look twice, check shoulders; stop, creep if blocked; never block.

why_how.text: Right-of-way rules set the order vehicles move through an intersection, and the law decides who must yield.
At a four-way stop the first to arrive goes first, and a near tie is settled by yielding to the right.
At a two-way stop the vehicle going straight has the right-of-way, and any turning driver yields to it.

narration.text: This lesson covers right-of-way at stop-controlled intersections. Right-of-way rules set the order in which vehicles move through an intersection, and the law decides who must yield, meaning give it up. We will cover the order at four-way stops, how near ties are settled, the rule for left turns at four-way stops, and who goes first at a two-way stop. These rules come up constantly in practice questions. To remember: what right-of-way means; four-way stops; two-way stops. A helpful hook for this lesson: first come first; tie goes right.

lines.text: Go in the order you arrived.
Near tie: left yields to right.

narration.text: At a four-way stop, vehicles go in the order they arrived. When two arrive at about the same time, the driver on the left yields to the one on the right. So the first rule is arrival order. At a four-way stop the first to arrive goes first, and only a near tie is settled by yielding to the vehicle on your right. The right-hand rule is a tie-breaker, not the main rule. To remember: go in the order you arrived; near tie: left yields to right; arrival order comes first. A helpful hook for this lesson: first come first; tie goes right.

At a four-way stop, a driver turning left must yield to vehicles going straight or turning right. So even at a four-way stop, a left turn carries an extra duty to yield. The arrival order and tie rules still apply, but a left-turning driver also waits for straight and right-turning traffic before making the turn. This is one of the turning rules that differs between four-way and two-way stops. To remember: left turners yield; to vehicles going straight; to vehicles turning right. A helpful hook for this lesson: first come first; tie goes right.

At a two-way stop, the vehicle going straight has the right-of-way, and turning vehicles must yield to it. A left-turning driver yields to straight and right-turning traffic at a four-way stop, while at a two-way stop any turning driver yields to the one going straight. So the two kinds of stop have different turning rules, and the question to ask is which kind of stop you are at. To remember: straight-through vehicle goes first; turning vehicles yield; different from four-way stop rules. A helpful hook for this lesson: first come first; tie goes right.

Here is the trap. Many drivers remember yield to the right and apply it to every four-way stop. At a four-way stop, vehicles go in the order they arrived. When two arrive at about the same time, the driver on the left yields to the one on the right. So a car on your right that arrived after you does not go first. The right-hand rule only settles a near tie. To remember: arrival order comes first; right-hand rule only breaks ties. A helpful hook for this lesson: first come first; tie goes right. In short: right-of-way rules set the order vehicles move through an intersection, and the law decides who must yield.

Here is a quick check: at a two-way stop, one car is going straight and another is turning. Who has the right-of-way? Decide before the answer. This is a two-way stop, not a four-way stop. The answer is the car going straight. At a two-way stop the vehicle going straight has the right-of-way, and turning vehicles must yield to it. A helpful hook for this lesson: first come first; tie goes right. In short: at a two-way stop the vehicle going straight has the right-of-way and turning vehicles must yield to it. In short: right-of-way rules set the order vehicles move through an intersection, and the law decides who must yield.

lines.text: Four-way: arrival order, tie to right.

narration.text: To close, right-of-way rules set the order through an intersection, and the law decides who must yield. At a four-way stop, vehicles go in arrival order, and in a near tie the driver on the left yields to the one on the right. A driver turning left at a four-way stop yields to vehicles going straight or turning right. At a two-way stop, the vehicle going straight has the right-of-way and turning vehicles yield. To remember: the law decides who yields; four-way: arrival order, tie to right; turners yield to straight traffic.

narration.text: This lesson covers turning. The guide sets a legal rule for which lane to turn into, explains how to handle more than one turn lane, and gives a signaling distance for turns across oncoming traffic. It also covers checking for bicyclists before you turn, and when a U-turn is and is not appropriate. Two of these rules carry exact limits that are worth memorizing. To remember: which lane to turn into; signals, gaps and bicyclists; U-turns. A helpful hook for this lesson: nearest lane first, then change. In short: washington law requires turning into the lane nearest the direction you came from, with lane changes only after the turn.

lines.text: Left or right turn: nearest lane.
Change lanes only after the turn.

narration.text: Washington law requires you to turn, left or right, into the lane nearest the direction you are coming from. You may change lanes only after finishing the turn. With more than one turn lane, stay in the same lane through the whole turn so you never drift into the next lane. So both rules keep your path predictable: end the turn in the nearest lane, and keep your own lane throughout a multiple-lane turn. To remember: left or right turn: nearest lane; change lanes only after the turn; multiple turn lanes: stay in yours.

lines.text: Signal at least one hundred feet ahead.

narration.text: Signal at least one hundred feet before turning left or right across oncoming traffic. Then wait for a safe gap, and check that the street you are entering is clear of vehicles, walkers and bicyclists. Signaling one hundred feet ahead is the minimum before a turn across oncoming traffic, and the turn itself must end in the lane nearest your starting side, with lane changes only afterward. To remember: signal at least one hundred feet ahead; wait for a safe gap; check the new street is clear. A helpful hook for this lesson: nearest lane first, then change.

lines.text: Never on a curve or near a hilltop.

narration.text: Check behind you for bicyclists and yield to them before you turn, since they may be closing on you faster than you think. In Washington a U-turn is generally legal unless a sign forbids it, but you need clear sight in every direction. So never make a U-turn on a curve or near the top of a hill. U-turns are allowed by default unless a sign bans them, yet a curve or an approaching hilltop still rules one out. To remember: check behind for bicyclists; U-turns generally legal unless banned; never on a curve or near a hilltop.

lines.text: Trap: U-turns need a sign to allow them.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Some drivers believe U-turns are illegal unless a sign permits them. The guide says the opposite. In Washington a U-turn is generally legal unless a sign forbids it. The limit is visibility: you need clear sight in every direction, so never make one on a curve or near the top of a hill. So the default is allowed, with a sign or a poor sightline as the two things that rule a U-turn out. To remember: allowed unless a sign bans them; curves and hilltops still rule them out. A helpful hook for this lesson: nearest lane first, then change. In short: signal at least one hundred feet before turning left or right across oncoming traffic.

Signal at least one hundred feet before turning across oncoming traffic, wait for a safe gap, and check the new street is clear. Check behind for bicyclists and yield to them. U-turns are generally legal unless a sign forbids them, but never on a curve or near a hilltop. To remember: nearest lane; change lanes after; signal one hundred feet ahead; U-turns legal unless banned or blind.

narration.text: This lesson covers the shapes intersections take and who has priority at each. The guide describes cross intersections, T-intersections and Y-intersections, and it covers mid-block crosswalks, which are crossings placed between intersections. Each shape has a clear rule for who goes first. Knowing the shape helps you know the rule even before you read the signs. To remember: cross intersections; T and Y intersections; mid-block crosswalks. A helpful hook for this lesson: ending or minor road waits. In short: at a T-intersection the through road has priority, and at a Y-intersection the major road has priority.

It may be controlled by lights, signs or markings, and you apply the right-of-way laws there. So at a cross intersection, the signals, stop signs or markings tell you what to do, and where they leave a question open, the right-of-way laws decide who goes first. To remember: four-way junction; at least one lane each way; lights, signs or markings; normal rules. A helpful hook for this lesson: ending or minor road waits. In short: at a T-intersection the through road has priority, and at a Y-intersection the major road has priority.

At a Y-intersection a minor road joins a major route, often with a stop sign on the minor road, and cars on the major road have the right-of-way. So in both shapes, the road that continues has priority. To remember: T: one road ends at a through road; Y: a minor road joins a major route; through or major road has priority. At a T-intersection through traffic has the right-of-way, and at a Y-intersection cars on the major road do, so the ending or minor road waits. At a mid-block crosswalk, pedestrians in a marked crosswalk always have the right-of-way, and drivers should stop for walkers and bicyclists even with no stop sign. narration.text: This short lesson covers traffic calming circles, the small circles found on many residential streets. They look a little like roundabouts but follow different rules. The guide describes how traffic moves around them, what signs they may have, which right-of-way rules apply, and how large vehicles use them. The main point is that calming circles use ordinary intersection rules. To remember: how they work; their signs and rules; large vehicles. A helpful hook for this lesson: counterclockwise, ordinary rules, big trucks may differ.

narration.text: A traffic calming circle has a painted or raised center island that traffic circles counterclockwise. It may post stop or yield signs on every approach, a few of them or none. It uses the ordinary right-of-way rules. So the signs you see, or the lack of them, tell you which ordinary rules apply, just as at any other intersection. To remember: painted or raised center island; traffic circles counterclockwise; signs on all, some or no approaches. So you still apply the normal right-of-way rules, and you watch for trucks or buses that may move in the opposite direction around the island. To remember: ordinary right-of-way rules apply; large vehicles may go clockwise. A helpful hook for this lesson: counterclockwise, ordinary rules, big trucks may differ.

That is the opposite of the counterclockwise direction other traffic uses. When you see a large vehicle at a calming circle, expect it to take an unusual path and give it the space it needs to get through. To remember: built for passenger cars; give fire trucks, buses, trucks room; they may go clockwise. A helpful hook for this lesson: counterclockwise, ordinary rules, big trucks may differ.

narration.text: This lesson covers roundabouts. The guide explains how they work, how large vehicles and bicyclists use them, what speeds they are designed for, how to choose a lane, and the steps for entering. It finishes with what to do if an emergency vehicle approaches while you are inside. Roundabouts are designed to serve cars, large trucks, buses, bicyclists and pedestrians alike, so each of these users has a part in this lesson. To remember: how roundabouts work; trucks and bicyclists; lanes, entry and emergencies. A helpful hook for this lesson: yield left, pick a lane, keep it.

lines.text: Designed for fifteen to twenty-five miles per hour.

narration.text: In a roundabout, every approaching vehicle yields on entry and then travels counterclockwise around a raised center island. Roundabouts are designed to serve cars, large trucks, buses, bicyclists and pedestrians alike. Slow down as you approach, because roundabouts are designed for speeds of fifteen to twenty-five miles per hour. So the pattern is the same each time: slow down, yield on entry, then circle counterclockwise. To remember: everyone yields on entry; travel counterclockwise around the island; designed for fifteen to twenty-five miles per hour.

lines.text: Trucks may use the apron and both lanes.

narration.text: Large vehicles may drive over a roundabout's truck apron and use both lanes, so give them plenty of space and stay well back from trucks. A bicyclist may ride through a roundabout either as a pedestrian or as a vehicle. When riding as a vehicle, the bicyclist should take the middle of the lane to be seen. So in a roundabout, expect trucks to take more room and bicyclists to ride in the center of a lane. To remember: trucks may use the apron and both lanes; give them plenty of space; bicyclists: pedestrian or vehicle.

lines.text: Stay in that lane to your exit.

So lane choice happens before you enter, not inside the circle. Once you are in the roundabout, you hold your lane all the way to your exit rather than changing lanes as you go around. To remember: read the lane choice sign; right turn, straight or left; stay in that lane to your exit. A helpful hook for this lesson: yield left, pick a lane, keep it. Entering a roundabout you look left and yield to traffic already circling, and once inside you hold your lane until your exit rather than changing lanes. To remember: stop for crosswalk users, entry and exit; look left; yield to circulating traffic; enter to the right at a gap. A helpful hook for this lesson: yield left, pick a lane, keep it.

narration.text: This final lesson of the section covers two special kinds of intersection. The diverging diamond is a newer Washington interchange design that changes which side of the road you drive on for a short stretch. The uncontrolled intersection is the opposite: an intersection with no signs at all, where the normal right-of-way rules decide who goes. We will cover how to drive each one. To remember: diverging diamond interchanges; uncontrolled intersections; who yields. A helpful hook for this lesson: minor road yields; diamond left turns flow.

lines.text: Traffic shifts to the opposite side.
Fewer crossing points, less crash risk.

narration.text: A diverging diamond is a newer Washington interchange that shifts traffic to the opposite side of the road so left turns onto and off freeway ramps flow better, with fewer crossing points and less crash risk. In a diverging diamond, markings and signals guide you to the left side of the road. You turn left onto the freeway without stopping or yielding to oncoming traffic, and you cross back to the right after the overpass or underpass. To remember: A newer Washington interchange; traffic shifts to the opposite side; fewer crossing points, less crash risk.

lines.text: Trap: stop and yield for the turn.
No stop for the freeway left turn.

narration.text: Here is the trap. On most roads, a left turn means yielding to oncoming traffic, so drivers expect to stop in a diverging diamond too. In a diverging diamond the left turn onto the freeway needs no stop and no yielding to oncoming traffic, because the design removes conflicts with oncoming vehicles, though you still follow the signs and markings. So the left turn onto the ramp flows without a stop. To remember: no stop for the freeway left turn; still follow signs and markings. A helpful hook for this lesson: minor road yields; diamond left turns flow.

lines.text: Usually on local roads and streets.

narration.text: An uncontrolled intersection has no signs. The normal right-of-way rules still apply, and such intersections are usually on local roads and streets. At an uncontrolled intersection you must yield if a vehicle is already in it, if you are entering or crossing a state highway from a secondary road, if you are moving from an unpaved to a paved road, or if you are turning left with a vehicle coming from the opposite direction. To remember: no signs at all; normal right-of-way rules apply; usually on local roads and streets.

lines.text: Secondary road yields to state highway.
Unpaved road yields to paved road.
Left turners yield to oncoming traffic.

narration.text: At an uncontrolled intersection the driver coming from a secondary or unpaved road yields to the one on the state highway or paved road. You also yield if a vehicle is already in the intersection, and when turning left with a vehicle coming from the opposite direction. So the pattern is that the smaller road yields to the larger one, and turning or late-arriving drivers yield to those already moving. To remember: secondary road yields to state highway; unpaved road yields to paved road; left turners yield to oncoming traffic.

Here is a quick check: in a diverging diamond, you are turning left onto the freeway. Do you stop and yield to oncoming traffic? Decide before the answer, and remember the trap. The answer is no. In a diverging diamond you turn left onto the freeway without stopping or yielding to oncoming traffic, because the design removes conflicts with oncoming vehicles, and you still follow the signs and markings. A helpful hook for this lesson: minor road yields; diamond left turns flow. In short: in a diverging diamond you turn left onto the freeway without stopping or yielding to oncoming traffic, following the signs and markings.

lines.text: Diamond: shift left, turn without stopping.

narration.text: To sum up, a diverging diamond shifts traffic to the opposite side of the road so freeway left turns flow better. Signals and markings guide you to the left side, you turn left onto the freeway without stopping or yielding to oncoming traffic, and you cross back after the overpass or underpass. At an uncontrolled intersection the normal rules apply: yield to vehicles already in it, to the state highway from a secondary road, to the paved road from an unpaved one, and to oncoming traffic when turning left. To remember: diamond: shift left, turn without stopping; uncontrolled: normal rules apply; minor and unpaved roads yield.
